Do Now: Input and Output

An input sends information into a computer. An output is information the computer sends back.

Complete the questions

steps.label: Build a Pong Game
steps.content:
iProgram

Build a Pong Game

Year 6, Lesson 2

steps.label: Today’s Task
steps.content:
Today’s Task

You will build a Pong-style game in TurboWarp.

  • The mouse controls a paddle.
  • A ball moves and bounces around the stage.
  • The game checks whether the ball touches the paddle.
  • Each successful hit increases the score and speed.

Finished when

Your paddle follows the mouse, the ball bounces, the score changes after a hit, and the game stops when the ball reaches the floor.

steps.label: Input, Process and Output
steps.content:
Input, Process and Output

A game repeatedly receives an input, processes it, and produces an output.

InputThe player moves the mouse.
ProcessThe program reads the mouse position.
OutputThe paddle moves on the screen.

Control

Control means directing what happens. In this game, the player controls the paddle while the program controls the ball, score, and rules.

steps.label: How Players Control Games
steps.content:
How Players Control Games

Different games receive different inputs. Identify the action the player performs in each example.

Your Pong game will use mouse movement as its input.

steps.label: Conditions and Decisions
steps.content:
Conditions and Decisions

A condition is a question with a true or false answer. An if block runs its instructions only when its condition is true.

Condition

Is the ball touching the paddle?

True: bounce and add one point.

False: keep moving.

if <touching [Paddle v] ?> then
change [score v] by (1)
end

The forever block makes the program check the condition again and again while the game runs.

steps.label: Open TurboWarp
steps.content:
Open TurboWarp

  1. Open TurboWarp using the button.
  2. Choose File, then New if another project appears.
  3. Delete the cat sprite.
  4. Save your project with the name Pong.

The Slides and TurboWarp switcher will stay at the top right. Use it whenever you need the next instruction.

Before moving on

You should have an empty project called Pong.

steps.label: Build the Stage
steps.content:
Build the Stage

  1. Select the Stage.
  2. Choose Backdrops, then use Paint.
  3. Fill the backdrop with a dark colour.
  4. Draw a thick red line across the stage near the bottom edge.
  5. Add a few small stars if there is time.

Why the red line?

The ball will use the red line as the game-over area. Keep enough space above it for the paddle.

CheckThe stage has a dark background and a clearly visible red floor.

steps.label: Create the Paddle
steps.content:
Create the Paddle

  1. Choose Paint from the Add Sprite button.
  2. Draw a wide, short rectangle.
  3. Use the centre tool so the cross is in the middle of the paddle.
  4. Name the sprite Paddle.
  5. Set its y position to -135.

Position

The y position controls height. A negative y value places the paddle below the centre of the stage.

CheckThe Paddle sits above the red floor and has room to move left and right.

steps.label: Code the Paddle
steps.content:
Code the Paddle

Select the Paddle sprite. Build this script from Events, Control, Motion, and Sensing.

when green flag clicked
set y to (-135)
forever
set x to (mouse x)
end

How it works

mouse x reports how far left or right the mouse is.

set x moves the paddle to the same horizontal position.

forever keeps updating the position.

TestPress the green flag and move the mouse. The paddle should follow from left to right.

steps.label: Create the Ball
steps.content:
Create the Ball

  1. Choose Paint from the Add Sprite button.
  2. Hold Shift while drawing a small circle.
  3. Place the centre cross in the middle.
  4. Name the sprite Ball.
  5. Set the size to about 25.

Important

Click the Ball in the sprite list before adding the next scripts. The blue outline shows which sprite you are coding.

CheckThe sprite list contains Paddle and Ball.

steps.label: Create Score and Speed
steps.content:
Create Score and Speed

A variable is a named place where a program stores a value that can change.

  1. Open Variables.
  2. Choose Make a Variable.
  3. Create score for all sprites.
  4. Create speed for all sprites.
  5. Leave score visible. Untick speed to hide its display.
set [score v] to (0)
set [speed v] to (5)

score stores successful paddle hits. speed stores how many steps the ball moves each time around the loop.

steps.label: Start the Ball
steps.content:
Start the Ball

Keep the Ball selected. This script resets the game and gives the ball a starting position and direction.

when green flag clicked
set [score v] to (0)
set [speed v] to (5)
go to x: (0) y: (130)
point in direction (135)

Starting values

The ball starts near the top centre. Direction 135 points down and right. Every new game starts with score 0 and speed 5.

TestMove the Ball elsewhere, press the green flag, and check that it returns to the top.

steps.label: Move and Bounce
steps.content:
Move and Bounce

Add a second script to the Ball. The variable speed goes inside the move block.

when green flag clicked
forever
if on edge, bounce
move (speed) steps
end

Sequence inside the loop

First the ball checks the edge. It then moves by the value stored in speed. The forever block repeats both instructions.

TestThe ball should move continuously and bounce from the top and side edges.

steps.label: Stop at the Floor
steps.content:
Stop at the Floor

Add this third script to the Ball. Click the colour square in the sensing block and use the colour picker to select your red floor.

when green flag clicked
wait until <touching color [#d62020] ?>
stop [all v]

Wait until

The program pauses at this block while the condition is false. As soon as the Ball touches the chosen colour, the condition becomes true and stop all ends the game.

TestMove the paddle away. The game should stop when the ball reaches the red floor.

steps.label: Bounce from the Paddle
steps.content:
Bounce from the Paddle

Add this fourth script to the Ball. Choose Paddle from the touching block menu.

when green flag clicked
forever
if <touching [Paddle v] ?> then
point in direction ((180) - (direction))
move (5) steps
end
end

The decision

The if block checks whether Ball touches Paddle. The subtraction points the ball upwards in the opposite vertical direction. Moving 5 steps separates the sprites so one hit is counted once.

TestCatch the ball with the paddle. It should travel upwards after contact.

steps.label: Add Score and Speed
steps.content:
Add Score and Speed

Place two variable blocks inside the if block, before the direction block.

when green flag clicked
forever
if <touching [Paddle v] ?> then
change [score v] by (1)
change [speed v] by (0.25)
point in direction ((180) - (direction))
move (5) steps
end
end

What changes?

Each paddle hit adds 1 to score. Adding 0.25 to speed makes every later move slightly larger, so the game becomes harder.

TestCatch the ball several times. The score should rise by one and the ball should gradually move faster.

steps.label: Test the Complete Game
steps.content:
Test the Complete Game

Test one requirement at a time. Fix each problem before moving to the next line.

Save

Save the project after all seven checks work.

steps.label: Debugging Guide
steps.content:
Debugging Guide

Paddle does not moveCheck that its script uses mouse x inside set x and sits inside forever.
Ball code moves the paddleSelect Ball in the sprite list before building the ball scripts.
Ball sticks to the paddleKeep move 5 steps after the direction block.
Score rises too quicklyCheck that change score by 1 is inside the touching Paddle if block.
Game ends too earlyUse the colour picker again and select only the red floor colour.
Ball does not get fasterPut the speed variable inside move and change speed by 0.25 after each hit.

steps.label: Extension: Less Predictable Bounces
steps.content:
Extension: Less Predictable Bounces

Make each paddle bounce slightly different by adding a random turn.

if <touching [Paddle v] ?> then
change [score v] by (1)
change [speed v] by (0.25)
point in direction ((180) - (direction))
turn cw (pick random (-20) to (20)) degrees
move (5) steps
end

Experiment

Try a smaller range such as -10 to 10, then a larger range such as -40 to 40. Choose values that keep the game playable.

ExtraAdd the Pen extension and make the Ball leave a short trail while it moves.

steps.label: Plenary
steps.content:
Plenary

Answer without using the instructions

y6l2_do_now.feedback: Look back at the definition above: which direction is the information travelling, into the game or out of it?
Look back at the definition above: is the game sending this information out, or receiving it?
Think of a physical device the player touches or moves to control the game, not something the screen shows them.

y6l2_plenary.feedback: Think about which block type makes a decision by checking whether something is true or false.
Think about how many times the game needs to check for contact while it's running - just once, or the whole time?
Work out how much the score changes for a single hit, then apply that to three hits.
